2561.prule: Root-initial stress: dynamic stress falls on the first syllable of di- and trisyllabic words ('normalement'), but a word-initial prefix that is not part of the root (examples: ka- in infinitives, me-/ki- in nouns) is skipped and stress lands on the following, root-initial syllable. Four-syllable words are mostly compounds or affixed roots; their construction determines stress, most commonly two stresses on syllables 1 and 3. The suffix -gara: counts as one syllable so the word takes the pattern of a shorter word. The source never mentions syllable weight or syllable structure as a stress factor; in its examples long vowels occur both stressed (/me'so:k/) and unstressed (/'coɡona:/, /'ŋa:mi:ɡara:/).
2561.srule: No primary/secondary distinction drawn. Di- and trisyllabic words carry one stress; four-syllable words (normally compounds or roots with affixes, whose construction influences stress) most commonly carry two unranked stresses on syllables 1 and 3 (/'jitna'kanak/ 'nine', /'përa:'ɡídoh/ 'millipede'); the suffix -gara: counts as one syllable, so /'ŋa:mi:ɡara: 'your cheek' has a single initial stress. 2562.prule: No Lehali-specific stress statement exists in any reachable source. Candidate reading, recorded but not adopted as a rule: final word stress, from François 2005's areal sentence 'in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable' (p.451), a hedged generalisation over the 17 Torres-Banks languages of Table 1 that never names Lehali. Lehali is a probable member of 'essentially all' (author's own 2004 Lehali data, fn.2; Table 4: LHI lost ALL posttonic vowels, the condition the sentence ties the stress shift to; ex.(29) Lehali reflexes of four-syllable etyma end in the historically stressed syllable), but the paper's own data and the catalog's adjudicated records show that the hedge covers real members of the same set: Hiw (last non-schwa vowel, weight-sensitive with a fixed default), Lo-Toga (same pattern, not determinable from the sources), Dorig ('otherwise a well-behaved oxytone language' but long /a/ 'tends to attract word stress', weight-sensitive, stated with hedges), Mota (kept non-high final vowels; Codrington's stem accent, set by morphology), Vera'a ('no stress', Schnell). So membership inference is not a statement about Lehali. Guy 1978 (PL C-61 p.782) adds only that word stress 'appears to have been innovated along different rules in Sakao, Lehali, and Shark Bay' and, in its Lehali correspondence table (pp.785-788), treats the PNNH vowel followed by a posttonic vowel as the Lehali tonic vowel, i.e. the same historical penult that François derives final stress; no synchronic position is given. 2567.heavy: The only eligible stress bearer is a vowel 'preceded by a consonant', i.e. a syllable with an onset ('the first vowel which is preceded by a consonant is stressed'); vowel length and coda consonants play no role in the statement.
2567.dflt: Not stated and does not arise in the data: every cited word has a post-consonantal vowel within its first two syllables; a word consisting of a bare vowel is not discussed.

tn.quote: Lhokpu 語には高調（high tone）と低調（low tone）の音韻論的対立が認められる。また contour tone として高昇調（rising tone）が観察される。また高調の異声調（allotone）として、形態素境界では下降調（falling tone）が現れる（[55] → [53] or [54] /____#）。ストレスや発声様式（phonation type）といった超分節音素はこの言語では弁別的ではない。音声レベルでは促声調にも高昇調が存在する。 ... 複音節語は第一音節が高調の場合は後の音節は低調に、第一音節が低調の場合は第二音節が高調になり第三音節は低調になる。
tn.translation: In Lhokpu a phonological opposition between high tone and low tone is recognised. A high-rising tone (rising tone) is also observed as a contour tone. As an allotone of the high tone, a falling tone appears at a morpheme boundary ([55] → [53] or [54] /____#). Suprasegmentals such as stress and phonation type are not distinctive in this language. At the phonetic level a high-rising tone also occurs on checked syllables. ... In polysyllabic words, when the first syllable is high the following syllables are low; when the first syllable is low the second becomes high and the third low.

Automatic contextual changes take place only in the interaction of adjacent high (H) and low (L) tones. In particular, the sequence LLH is replaced by LHL: bàà 'goat' fàlá 'two' — bàà fálà. 2572.heavy: Main stress is not weight-conditioned. 2572.prule: One main stress per word, located on the stem (root): 'in almost all cases, main stress falls on the stem'; prefixes 'never bear main stress' and suffixes/enclitics are unstressed. Placement is by morphological constituency, not by syllable count or weight.
2572.srule: Secondary stress on every non-initial bimoraic (trochaic) foot: after the main-stressed stem syllable, a heavy syllable is footed and carries secondary stress when a bimoraic suffix/enclitic follows a consonant (the consonant geminates: [a'njumˌˌme:], ['tʰaŋˌŋaŋˌŋã:], [kɛ'siraˌdhaŋˌˌŋi:]); light monomoraic syllables stay unfooted with no secondary stress ([kɛ'nisiŋi]).

2573.heavy: No weight conditioning stated; long vowels and diphthongs are treated as single nuclei that carry penultimate stress as a whole, not as heavy syllables attracting stress.
2573.prule: Stress on the penultimate syllable of the stem word ('stamwoord'), whether a bare base or a base plus prefixes/infixes/suffixes (-i, -a, -ka, -aka shift stress rightward so that it stays penultimate). Enclitic particles, interjectional pronouns and possessive enclitics are outside the domain and do not move stress (bónekoe, béngkana, hóoe-kami). Two syllabification provisions: a long vowel formed by antepenult+penult vowels is stressed as a whole (-daai), as is a long vowel formed by penult and final vowels (roeaa 'klemtoon op de lange a', -woerii 'klemtoon op de lange i'), and when the penult is a single vowel forming a diphthong with the preceding vowel, stress sits on the first element (nampopóida, -wáika, ka-láoea), 'as in Ledo'.

2575.tone: Six syllabic tones: i low-rising legato with final laryngeal constriction, ii high-level legato, iii mid-level legato, iv low-falling legato (on open/vowel/nasal-final syllables); v high-level staccato, vi mid-level staccato (only on syllables ending in -?, -p, -t, -k). Neutralization: suffixes and enclitics lose their tone and take the mid-level contour (tone iii); recent Mandarin loans take a 'non-committal' mid tone. Sandhi: tone i is low-rising+constricted only in isolation or phrase-finally, low-falling elsewhere; tone iv becomes mid-level in the same non-final position. The only occurrence of the word 'accent' is 'the syllabic musical accent or tone (T)'; 'stress' does not occur. No stress or accentual prominence is described.

2578.quote: Die Betonung der Worte erfolgt immer auf der vorletzten Silbe. The transcription also marks the boundaries of intonation groups by a short vertical sign |. Intonation contours are not represented, but a distinction is made between the nuclear stress of the intonation group and non-nuclear stress.

2580.prule: Stress position is set by word class and morphological base, not by syllable count or weight. (a) Nominals (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, numerals) and most adverbials: word-final stress is the basic position (citation form, pre-pausal), e.g. +šultanà 'king', bratà 'girl', with retraction to the penult in non-pausal position mid intonation group; annexation forms, noš- 'self' + suffix, vocatives and a few adverbs (+rába, bára) are penultimate. (b) Verbs from the present base, past bases and imperative: stress on the syllable whose vowel nucleus precedes the final root radical (+qatə́l 'he kills', +qtə́lle 'he killed', +dmíx 'he has slept', +qtúl 'kill!'), or on the first suffix syllable if that vowel is elided (+qatlá 'she kills', +qatlét); (c) compound verb forms on a resultative-participle or infinitive base stress the syllable after the final radical, the nominal pattern (+qtilé 'he has killed', +qatolé 'he is killing'). Further pronominal/TAM suffixes leave the stress in place (+qatə́llu 'he kills them', +qatə́lwalu, +qatlíwalu).

2581.prule: Right-edge, weight-conditioned at the final syllable: primary stress on the final syllable if it contains a vowel sequence (two vowels) or a long vowel, otherwise on the penultimate syllable. Closed final syllables with a short vowel do not attract stress ([nou'tiret], ['mbəmən]). Syllable count is over the whole inflected word (prefixes and suffixes included) and shifts rightward under suffixation; schwa syllables (including prefix-final schwa) count and can bear stress, syllabic nasals/liquids count as nuclei ([nə'vern]), but schwas eligible for optional deletion (sec. 2.1.2.2) are skipped in the count, so stress can surface on the final syllable ([gə'lo]) or on a full-syllable prefix (['kəgəlo ~ 'kəglo]).

2582.tone: Two-level tone language (H, L). p. 417: contour tones (rising nìkǎ 'cow'; falling tébê(ŋ̀) 'border', káî 'hoe', yíâ 'dog', ɔ̀fɔ̂(ŋ̀) 'spirit', pùpû 'ant') are posited underlyingly and surface as level H or L depending on context (Spears reports some surface contours); TBU is the mora underlyingly and the syllable on the surface; super-high tone only in intensifying ideophones (tànı̋ı̋ 'very (small)'), possibly intonational; six nominal tonal classes after Dwyer 1973, verbs tentatively four; grammatical tone = lowering of the second member of a nominal construction (replacement of its lexical tone by L) with advancement of the first member's final H. 2583.prule: No contrastive stress; three-tone language (21/33/55). Perceived stress (= loudness) tracks tone height: in a two-syllable utterance the higher-toned syllable is slightly stronger, equal tones give equal stress; no vowel lengthening under stress. No positional stress rule; the only positional effect is final-syllable stress (with pitch raised 55 -> 66) in a closed set of time-adverbial phrases ('then; later; next; at that time').
